meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Biggest damfool mistake I ever made'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Eisenhower on appointing Earl Warren. No letter, diary or transcript records it — and his biographer wrote that Eisenhower never said it.

answer.label: Unsourced — commonly credited to
answer.sourceLine: Eisenhower’s souring on Chief Justice Earl Warren is genuinely documented — the snappy sentence is not. No letter, diary entry, transcript or recording preserves him saying it; the citation trail reference works offer stops at a secondhand report in a 1968 magazine essay, and his biographer Jean Edward Smith wrote in 2012 that “Eisenhower never said that. I have no evidence that he ever made such a statement.”

source.excerpt: Biggest damfool mistake I ever made.
trail: A period printing exists: TIME told readers on 22 July 1974 ↗ that “Ike described the selection as ‘the biggest damn fool mistake I ever made.’” TIME gives no source for it.

Theo Lippman Jr. traced the family of Eisenhower-on-Warren quips for The Baltimore Sun on 7 September 1997 ↗ and found the documentary residue thin: Justice Harold Burton’s diary records only that Eisenhower “expressed disappointment at the trend of decisions of Chief Justice and Brennan,” while the Eisenhower Library “says it has found no corroboration of Eisenhower’s uttering such a quote, in that or any other instance.”

Wikipedia’s article on Earl Warren ↗ hedges the line to “some writers believe,” and footnotes Jean Edward Smith, Eisenhower in War and Peace (Random House, 2012), p. 603n: “Eisenhower never said that. I have no evidence that he ever made such a statement.”

The Virginia Law Weekly, surveying the same competing versions on 17 October 2018 ↗, cited none of them to a source and concluded simply that “Historians argue whether or not Eisenhower ever said any of the above.”
source.excerptNote: There is no transcript, letter or diary entry to quote from — the line circulates as a bare sentence with no surrounding words. The closest thing to a period setting is TIME’s account of 22 July 1974 ↗, which framed it this way: “Later, dismayed that Warren turned out to be a controversial participant rather than a bland umpire, Ike described the selection as ‘the biggest damn fool mistake I ever made.’” Note that even there the wording is “damn fool,” not the contracted “damfool” of the version usually quoted.

sourceLink.text: TIME, “Earl Warren’s Way: Is It Fair?” (22 July 1974)

source.rightsNote: No source work has ever been identified for this sentence — no speech, letter, diary or interview transcript — so there is nothing whose first-publication date could settle a copyright status. Quotle.info therefore asserts none; the fragment is reproduced here for identification and for commentary on the attribution itself.

author.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
author.kicker: The man it is pinned on
author.heading: Who Eisenhower actually was
author.metaLine: 1890–1969 · Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, then 34th President of the United States
author.bio: Dwight David Eisenhower commanded the Allied invasion of Europe before serving two terms in the White House, from January 1953 to January 1961. In October 1953 he installed California governor Earl Warren as Chief Justice of the United States — a court that went on to hand down Brown v. Board of Education and a run of decisions Eisenhower, a temperamental gradualist, found far bolder than he had bargained for. His private irritation with Warren is well attested; the pithy sentence the internet keeps handing him is not.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the attribution
misattribution.intro: The man is probably the right man; the sentence is the problem. Eisenhower really did sour on Earl Warren — but the crisp epigram everyone repeats has never been tied to anything he is recorded as saying.

items.why: No document produces it. The citation trail assembled by reference works stops at Fred Rodell’s essay “The Complexities of Mr. Justice Fortas,” The New York Times Magazine, 28 July 1968, p. 12 — a law professor’s magazine piece reporting the remark, not Eisenhower saying it. (Wikiquote files the line under ‘Disputed’ ↗ with exactly that citation — adding that Eisenhower’s memoirs assistant William B. Ewald Jr. heard a different, blunter version at Gettysburg in 1961 — and a quotation database ↗ reproduces it too; Quotle.info was not able to read the 1968 article itself and does not vouch for what it contains.) Wikipedia’s Earl Warren article ↗ quotes biographer Jean Edward Smith’s verdict: “Eisenhower never said that.”

Even the people repeating it cannot agree on the words. TIME in 1974 ↗ and American Heritage in 2003 ↗ print “damn fool” and “damn-fool”; the contracted “damfool” belongs to the reference-book version. A line with no fixed text is a line with no transcript behind it.

items.who: “I made two mistakes and both of them are sitting on the Supreme Court”
items.why: Usually quoted alongside it, and no better founded. Theo Lippman Jr. reported for The Baltimore Sun ↗ that the Eisenhower Library “says it has found no corroboration of Eisenhower’s uttering such a quote, in that or any other instance,” and that the diary entry cited as its source says only that Eisenhower “expressed disappointment at the trend of decisions of Chief Justice and Brennan.”

American Heritage ran it in its August/September 2003 issue ↗ as settled history with no source; George Parry opened a 2017 Philadelphia Inquirer commentary ↗ with the bare sentence. Neither says where Eisenhower said it.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented residue is smaller and duller than the epigram: Justice Harold Burton’s diary records only that Eisenhower “expressed disappointment at the trend of decisions of Chief Justice and Brennan,” and the Eisenhower Library reported finding no corroboration ↗ of the ‘two mistakes’ version.

context.heading: Why this one keeps getting quoted
lead: It is the founding text of a whole genre of American political writing: the president who picks a judge and lives to regret it. Eisenhower gave Earl Warren the centre chair in October 1953 expecting a steady administrator, and got the court of Brown v. Board of Education. A one-sentence expression of buyer’s remorse is exactly what that story needs, so the story supplied one.

The underlying feeling is real enough — Eisenhower’s private impatience with Warren is attested by people who were around him. What is missing is the sentence. Almost every time it is printed, it is printed bare: no date, no room, no listener, no transcript. That is the signature of a line that grew in the retelling rather than one that was written down.
detailsBody: Warren took his seat as Chief Justice on 5 October 1953 under a recess appointment dated 2 October, and was confirmed by the Senate in March 1954; he served until 23 June 1969. Eisenhower died on 28 March 1969.

Two related remarks are better attested than the famous one, and neither is quotable in the same way. William B. Ewald Jr., who worked on Eisenhower’s memoirs, reported hearing him say at Gettysburg in 1961 that his two worst appointments came out of Justice Department recommendations, naming the head of the Antitrust Division and Earl Warren. And Justice Burton’s diary records only “disappointment at the trend of decisions.” Neither has ever displaced the tidier one-liner.
context.pull: Eisenhower’s regret is real. The sentence isn’t sourced.
